title: Tell me about your weekend
goal: Link sentences into a whole story with subordinate clauses — and master one last big exception: *ikke* moving forward.
bekal: move *ikke* in front of the verb inside a subordinate clause
tell a longer story and end a conversation naturally
wave: Review **unit 18** first: read the Aarhus trip story out loud, then retell it without looking at the text.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Den sidste time
dialogs.intro: The last day of the course. The teacher asks everyone to talk about their weekend — this time in long sentences.

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Sidste opgave: fortæl om jeres weekend. Men brug lange sætninger.
lines.id: Last task: tell us about your weekend. But use long sentences.
lines.literal: last task: tell about your(pl.) weekend. but use long sentences.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Jeg blev hjemme, fordi jeg var syg. Det var kedeligt.
lines.id: I stayed home because I was sick. It was boring.
lines.literal: I stayed home, because I was sick. it was boring.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jeg tror ikke, at det var kedeligt. Du så seks film.
lines.id: I don't think it was boring. You watched six films.
lines.literal: I believe not, that it was boring. you saw six films.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Fordi jeg ikke kunne gøre andet!
lines.id: Because I couldn't do anything else!
lines.literal: because I not could do other!

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: God sætning, Mette. Hørte I, hvor ikke stod?
lines.id: Good sentence, Mette. Did you hear where *ikke* was?
lines.literal: good sentence, Mette. heard you(pl.), where not stood?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Før verbet. Fordi jeg **ikke kunne** — ikke efter.
lines.id: Before the verb. *Fordi jeg ikke kunne* — not after it.
lines.literal: before verb-the. because I not could — not after.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg tog til Malmø med Ahmad, fordi vi begge havde fri.
lines.id: I went to Malmö with Ahmad, because we both had the day off.
lines.literal: I took to Malmö with Ahmad, because we both had free.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Da vi kom frem, regnede det. Men det gjorde ikke noget.
lines.id: When we got there, it was raining. But that was okay.
lines.literal: when we came forth, rained it. but it did not anything.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vi fandt en café, hvor de spillede gammel dansk musik. I Sverige!
lines.id: We found a café where they were playing old Danish music. In Sweden!
lines.literal: we found a café, where they played old Danish music. in Sweden!

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Og hvis du spørger mig, var det den bedste del af turen.
lines.id: And if you ask me, that was the best part of the trip.
lines.literal: and if you ask me, was it the best part of trip-the.

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Det er den slags sætninger, jeg har ventet på hele semestret.
lines.id: That's the kind of sentence I've been waiting for all semester.
lines.literal: it is the kind sentences, I have waited on whole semester-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tak for i dag. Og tak for hele kurset.
lines.id: Thanks for today. And thanks for the whole course.
lines.literal: thanks for today. and thanks for whole course-the.

notes: **Fordi jeg ikke kunne** — this is the core of the unit. Inside a subordinate clause, *ikke* comes **before** the verb, not after it. Compare: *Jeg kunne ikke* (main clause) with *fordi jeg ikke kunne* (subordinate clause).

**Jeg tror ikke, at det var kedeligt.** Notice the negative moves to the main clause. Danish, like English, prefers to negate *tror* ("I don't think…") rather than the content of the clause. *Jeg tror, at det ikke var kedeligt* is correct but sounds stiff.

**Da vs når.** Both mean "when". **Da** is for a single event in the past: *Da vi kom frem, regnede det.* **Når** is for repeated events or the future: *Når det regner, tager jeg bussen.* The division is strict and the two can't be swapped.

**Da vi kom frem, regnede det** — the subordinate clause takes first place, so the main clause swaps subject and verb. The verb-second rule from unit 10 treats the whole subordinate clause as **one** first-place item.

**Som** and **hvor** link descriptions: *en café, **hvor** de spillede musik* (a café where they played music), *manden, **som** står der* (the man who's standing there). *Som* can often be dropped when it isn't the subject: *filmen (som) jeg så* — just like English "the film (that) I saw".
**Begge** = both. *Vi begge*, *begge to*, *begge dele* (both, for things).
**Den slags** = that kind, that sort. *En slags* = a kind of. Very useful when you don't know the name of something: *Det er en slags kage.*
**Tak for i dag** — the standard closing at the end of a class, meeting or workday. Joins *tak for i aften*, *tak for hjælpen*, *tak for sidst* from unit 7.

grammars.title: Subordinate clauses: ikke moves forward
body: This is the last exception you need to master at A1, and it's the only place where the *ikke* rule from unit 10 doesn't apply.
After certain linking words, a sentence becomes a **subordinate clause** — and inside it, adverbs like *ikke*, *altid*, *aldrig*, *også* move **in front of** the verb.
after: Linking words that start a subordinate clause: **at** (that), **fordi** (because), **hvis** (if), **når** (when, repeated), **da** (when, once in the past), **som/der** (who, which), **hvor** (where), **før** (before), **efter at** (after), **selvom** (although), **mens** (while).

⚠️ Compare the coordinating conjunctions from unit 10 — *og*, *men*, *eller*, *for*, *så* — which **don't** change anything. *Jeg kommer ikke, **for** jeg er syg* (normal order) vs *Jeg kommer ikke, **fordi** jeg **ikke** har tid* (ikke moves).
How to remember it: the moment you hear yourself say *at*, *fordi*, *hvis* or *når*, get *ikke* ready to **step forward**.

grammars.title: Subordinate clause in first place
body: A subordinate clause can come before the whole sentence. When it does, it fills first place — and the subject of the main clause jumps behind the verb, exactly like time expressions in unit 10.

head: Order
Example
rows: Vi blev hjemme, **fordi hun var syg**.
**Fordi hun var syg**, blev vi hjemme.
Det var det bedste, **hvis du spørger mig**.
**Hvis du spørger mig**, var det det bedste.

after: Notice the comma before the verb in the even rows. Danish uses far more commas than English, and the comma before a subordinate clause is **required** by the official rules.
This structure sounds more mature and flows better than a string of short sentences. If you want to take your Danish up a level with a single change, this is the change.

head: Dansk
Meaning
Type
Example
rows: Jeg vil, men jeg kan ikke.
Jeg går, for jeg er træt.
Det regner, så vi bliver hjemme.
Jeg ved, at han ikke kommer.
Hvis du vil, kan vi gå.
Når det regner, cykler jeg ikke.
Mens du laver mad, dækker jeg bord.
Før jeg går, rydder jeg op.

blocks.text: *Som* and *der* both mean "who, which". *Der* can only be the subject (*manden, der bor her*); *som* can be either. When in doubt, use *som* — it's always right.

sections.title: Telling stories and ending a conversation

blocks.text: You already have all the tools. What's left are the little phrases that keep a story flowing and let a conversation end naturally.
*Nå* is the hardest word to translate and one Danes say constantly. It marks a transition: "oh", "well", "right then", depending on the tone. *Nå?* with a rising tone means "and?".
*Jeg er ked af det* = I'm sad / I'm sorry. Used for deeper regret than *undskyld*.

blocks.title: You've reached the end of A1
items: Twenty units ago, you couldn't say *jeg*. Now you can introduce yourself, shop, order food, tell the time, ask for directions, give your opinion, talk about yesterday, and build long sentences with subordinate clauses in the right word order.
What's left isn't new material but **practice hours**. Danish doesn't surrender to people who read it; it surrenders to people who say it out loud, again and again, for months.
The "What's next" page at the back of this book gives four steps that really move the needle. Read it now, while everything is still fresh.
*Tak for nu — og held og lykke!*

exercises.prompt: Join into one sentence using the linking word in brackets.
items: Jeg blev hjemme. Jeg var syg. (fordi)
Jeg ved det. Han kommer i morgen. (at)
Det regner. Jeg cykler alligevel. (selvom)
Du vil. Vi kan gå nu. (hvis)
Vi fandt en café. De spillede dansk musik. (hvor)

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: kommer / at / han / ved / ikke / jeg / ,
syg / fordi / hjemme / jeg / var / blev / jeg / ,
regner / det / når / bussen / tager / jeg / ,
frem / da / kom / regnede / vi / det / ,
ved / snakkes / vi

answers: Jeg ved, at han ikke kommer. — Han kommer ikke i dag. — Jeg bliver hjemme, fordi jeg ikke har tid. — Hvis det ikke regner, cykler jeg. — Jeg tror ikke, at hun er syg.
Jeg blev hjemme, fordi jeg var syg. — Jeg ved, at han kommer i morgen. — Selvom det regner, cykler jeg alligevel. — Hvis du vil, kan vi gå nu. — Vi fandt en café, hvor de spillede dansk musik.
Jeg ved, at han ikke kommer. — Jeg blev hjemme, fordi jeg var syg. — Når det regner, tager jeg bussen. — Da vi kom frem, regnede det. — Vi snakkes ved.
